prompt: Why does a 1° alcohol undergo HBr conversion via SN2 while a 3° alcohol goes via SN1?

options.label: A 3° carbocation is stable enough to form freely; a 1° carbocation is too unstable, forcing concerted backside attack.
A 1° alcohol has less steric hindrance at carbon, so Br⁻ can reach it concertedly, while 3° is too hindered for backside attack.
A 3° OH is more basic than a 1° OH, so it's protonated more readily and ionizes to the cation first.
The C–O bond is weaker in 3° alcohols than in 1°, so it breaks ionically before Br⁻ attacks.

explanation: Both substrates protonate first (H₂O becomes the LG). 3° gives a stable 3° carbocation → SN1. 1° can't support an unstable 1° cation, so Br⁻ attacks concertedly as H₂O leaves → SN2. Both A and B are factors — but cation stability is the dominant driver. 2° can go either way.
